subject: NT
question: Discuss the healing of the paralytic (Mark 2:1-12) and compare it with the faith required for spiritual healing in contemporary Christian practices.
idealAnswer: Mark chapter 2 opens with further glimpses of Jesus’ ministry of miracles and teaching. A few days after Jesus’ arrival in Capernaum it was reported that He was at home, possibly Peter’s house, and while He was speaking a paralytic was brought by friends. Determined to get Jesus’ attention, they made an opening in the roof and lowered the disabled man through it on a mat right in front of Him. Jesus considered the determined effort of the four as visible evidence of their faith in His ability or power to heal the man, and in healing the paralytic He said, "son your sins are forgiven". In the Old Testament, disease and death were viewed as the consequences of man’s sinful condition, and healing was predicated on God’s forgiveness. This does not mean that there is a corresponding sin for each occurrence of sickness; Jesus simply showed that this man’s physical condition had a basic spiritual cause. The scribes expected a physical healing, but Jesus pronounced the man’s sins forgiven — He did not even say "you are healed" but made a simple pronouncement of forgiveness. To the Jewish leaders this was blasphemy, claiming to do something only God could do, an offence that attracted the death penalty. Jesus then calls Himself Son of Man. The title "Son of man" emphasizes that Jesus is fully human, while Son of God emphasizes deity, that is, He is fully God. As God’s Son, Jesus has the authority to forgive sin; as a man He can identify with our deepest sufferings and help us overcome sin. For Christian practice today the passage teaches that healing is sought from the One who has authority both to forgive and to heal, that the persistent, costly faith of a believer’s friends and intercessors counts before Christ, and that the deepest healing anyone needs is the forgiveness of sins rather than the removal of a physical complaint — while remembering that not every sickness is the result of a particular sin.

Jesus took the determined effort of the four as visible evidence of their faith in His power to heal
Jesus said "son your sins are forgiven" instead of pronouncing a physical cure
In the Old Testament disease and death were consequences of man’s sinful condition and healing was predicated on God’s forgiveness
Not every sickness has a corresponding sin; Jesus showed this man’s condition had a basic spiritual cause
The scribes judged the pronouncement blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins, an offence carrying the death penalty
"Son of man" emphasizes Jesus’ full humanity and "Son of God" His deity; as God’s Son He has authority to forgive sin
Application: intercessory faith, dependence on Christ’s authority, and forgiveness as the deepest healing in Christian practice today

subject: NT
question: Discuss Jesus’ teaching on marriage and divorce (Mark 10:1-12) and compare it with same-sex marriage.
idealAnswer: The question the Pharisees put to Jesus about divorce was malicious: it was put in order to test Him, that is, to try to induce Him to incriminate Himself by contradicting the Mosaic Law. The Mosaic enactment of Deuteronomy 24:1-4 stated that a husband was allowed to divorce his wife by writing and giving her a certificate of divorce if he had found some unseemly thing in her, and the question turned upon what constituted an unseemly thing. Shammai and Hillel were the authorities in the interpretation of the Mosaic Law, and different groups took their authority from them. The school of Shammai maintained the strict interpretation, that the marriage bond was indissoluble except in the event of the wife’s infidelity, while the school of Hillel took the liberal view, allowing divorce for almost any cause. In reply, Jesus first pointed out that Moses’ legislation was a concession to human weakness, rightly introduced to regulate divorce in a defective state of society: "Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote to you this commandment." Secondly, Jesus took them back beyond Moses to God’s ideal at the beginning of creation, from which we discover that marriage was instituted as the divine ideal for man and woman, and that the bond is permanent and indissoluble. Measured against that teaching, a same-sex union cannot be marriage in the sense Jesus gives it: He grounds marriage not in the concession of Moses nor in the customs of any age, but in the creation of man and woman, and He holds the bond that joins them to be permanent. A Lay Preacher must therefore teach marriage as God’s ideal for man and woman, while showing the pastoral compassion that Jesus showed to those whose lives fall short of it.
keyPoints: The Pharisees’ question was malicious, put to test Jesus and induce Him to contradict the Mosaic Law
Deuteronomy 24:1-4 allowed a husband to divorce his wife with a certificate for "some unseemly thing"
The dispute turned on what constituted an unseemly thing
The school of Shammai held the bond indissoluble except for the wife’s infidelity; the school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any cause
Jesus said Moses’ legislation was a concession to human weakness because of the hardness of their hearts
Jesus took them back beyond Moses to God’s ideal at creation
Marriage was instituted as the divine ideal for man and woman, and the bond is permanent and indissoluble
Comparison: Jesus roots marriage in the creation of man and woman, which excludes same-sex marriage from that definition

subject: NT
topic: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
question: Discuss Jesus’ judgement on the misuse of the Temple (Mark 12:15-19) and compare it with present-day worship in Chapels.
idealAnswer: When Jesus arrived in Jerusalem He went into the temple area. There was a large outer court of the Gentiles surrounding the inner sacred courts of the temple itself, and no Gentile was allowed beyond this outer court. In it the High Priest Caiaphas had authorized a market for the sale of ritually pure items necessary for temple sacrifice: wine, oil, salt, approved sacrificial animals and birds. The merchants, and the money changers who exchanged various currencies for the kind of coinage accepted for paying the annual Temple tax, apparently turned the Court of the Gentiles into some sort of bazaar, making it impossible for any Gentile to use the area for prayer or serious devotion to God. Jesus was outraged by this blatant disregard for the temple area specifically set apart for Gentile use. He therefore overturned the tables of the money changers, and would also not allow people to use the area as a thoroughfare. Jesus’ action captured people’s attention, and He used the occasion to teach them about God’s purpose for the temple, intended also as a house of prayer for all nations. Mark sandwiches this story inside the story of the barren fig tree, whose leaves promised fruit that was not there; both episodes signify God’s impending judgment on Israel for religious hypocrisy, for the Temple had the appearance of dedication to God while the substance fell short of doing His will. Compared with worship in our Chapels today, the passage warns against trading and money-raising that crowd out prayer, against turning the house of God into a thoroughfare or a market, against excluding any group of worshippers from the place set apart for them, and against an outward appearance of dedication that is not matched by obedience to God’s will.
keyPoints: Jesus entered the temple area, where the outer Court of the Gentiles surrounded the inner sacred courts
No Gentile was allowed beyond the outer court
Caiaphas the High Priest had authorized a market there for ritually pure items for sacrifice — wine, oil, salt, animals and birds
Merchants and money changers, who changed currency for the annual Temple tax, turned the court into a bazaar
This made it impossible for any Gentile to use the area for prayer or serious devotion
Jesus was outraged at the disregard for the area set apart for Gentile use, overturned the tables and stopped its use as a thoroughfare
He taught that the temple was intended also as a house of prayer for all nations
The sandwiched fig tree story shows the Temple had the appearance of dedication but fell short of God’s will — judgment on religious hypocrisy
Application: trading and fund-raising must not crowd out prayer, and no worshipper should be shut out of the Chapel

subject: NT
question: Discuss the Administration in the Church (Acts 6:1-7): how the Church addressed the Greek-speaking Christians’ complaint against the Hebrews concerning the distribution of supplies. What recommendation can you make for the improvement of your local Society’s Welfare system?
idealAnswer: In the Jewish world tensions existed between the Grecian Jews, the Hellenists, and the Aramaic-speaking Jews, the Hebrews, and unfortunately these strains were brought into the church. The Greek-speaking Christians complained against the Hebrews that their widows were neglected in the distribution of supplies. The apostles accepted the criticism, which in reality was directed against them, but they recognized that their first priority was the ministry of the word of God and prayer. They therefore gave the Greek-speaking Christians a share in the administration: seven assistants were appointed, all of them Hellenists, judging from their names, and they were commissioned with the full blessing of the Twelve. The solution was timely and yielded positive results, for the word of God spread and the number of disciples increased. The most outstanding member of the seven was Stephen, who became a key figure in early Christian history and had a grasp of the universal character of the Gospel; another prominent member was Philip, who carried the Gospel to Samaria and West Judea. For a local Society’s welfare system the passage recommends that complaints of neglect be heard rather than dismissed; that those who feel neglected be given a share in the administration rather than merely being pacified; that people of good standing be appointed and properly commissioned by the leadership; and that preachers and ministers keep their first priority, the ministry of the word and prayer, while the welfare work is entrusted to those appointed for it.
keyPoints: Tensions between Hellenists (Grecian Jews) and Hebrews existed in the Jewish world and were brought into the church
The Greek-speaking Christians complained that their widows were neglected in the distribution of supplies
The apostles accepted the criticism, which was in reality directed against them
They recognized their first priority as the ministry of the word of God and prayer
They gave the Hellenists a share in the administration — seven assistants, all Hellenists by their names
The seven were commissioned with the full blessing of the Twelve
The solution was timely and yielded positive results
Stephen and Philip were the outstanding members of the seven
Recommendations for a Society welfare system: hear complaints, share administration, appoint and commission suitable people, protect the ministry of word and prayer

subject: NT
question: "Now there is great gain in godliness with contentment" (1 Timothy 6:6). Discuss the statement with regard to the acquisition of wealth.
idealAnswer: Paul is answering false teachers who think that piety is mere gain, forgetting to add the qualification of contentment. In verse 6 we read: "There is a great gain in godliness with contentment." Picking up the words "godliness" and "gain", Paul shifted their meaning from the erroneous to the truthful. Godliness does not give financial gain; it is a gain when it is accompanied with contentment. Godliness without contentment would give a one-sided testimony, and contentment without godliness would not be distinctively Christian at all. Paul then contrasts the proper attitude of contentment with its opposite, the craving to get rich and the love of money. The grasping after riches leads people to fall into temptation, into a snare, and into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and destruction. With regard to the acquisition of wealth, therefore, the Christian is not forbidden to work or to own, but is warned that wealth is not the measure of godliness and that the desire to be rich is a trap. True profit lies in a godly life held together with a contented spirit; the preacher who teaches that piety brings riches has fallen into the very error Paul is correcting.
keyPoints: The false teachers thought that piety is mere gain, forgetting the qualification of contentment

Godliness does not give financial gain; it is gain when accompanied with contentment
Godliness without contentment gives a one-sided testimony
Contentment without godliness would not be distinctively Christian at all
Paul contrasts contentment with the craving to get rich and the love of money
Grasping after riches leads to temptation, a snare, and senseless and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and destruction

markingRubric.label: The error being corrected
markingRubric.description: Explains that the false teachers thought piety was mere gain and left out the qualification of contentment, and that Paul shifted the meaning of "godliness" and "gain" from the erroneous to the truthful.

markingRubric.label: Godliness with contentment
markingRubric.description: States that godliness does not give financial gain but is gain when accompanied with contentment; godliness without contentment gives a one-sided testimony and contentment without godliness is not distinctively Christian.

markingRubric.label: The craving to get rich
markingRubric.description: Contrasts contentment with the craving to get rich and the love of money, which leads people into temptation, a snare, and senseless and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and destruction.

markingRubric.label: Application to the acquisition of wealth
markingRubric.description: Applies the teaching: wealth is not the measure of godliness, the desire to be rich is a trap, and true profit is a godly life held with a contented spirit.

explanation: Tests the candidate’s understanding of 1 Timothy 6:6 as the syllabus expounds it and its bearing on the acquisition of wealth.

manualReference.excerpt: It is a gain when accompanied with contentment. In other words, godliness without contentment would give a one-sided testimony.
